evaluations.name: Fully-paid securities lending on your own long holdings (be the lender)
evaluations.mechanics: You own shares; you enroll them in a broker's fully-paid lending program (IBKR Stock Yield Enhancement, Fidelity Fully Paid Lending, Schwab Fully Paid). When a short seller needs to borrow, the broker lends YOUR shares and you collect a share of the borrow fee accrued daily on the collateral value (SYEP fee = Collateral x rate / 360). You keep full economic price exposure — you still profit/lose on the stock exactly as before — so the fee is genuinely INCREMENTAL carry. Verified structure: SEC Rule 15c3-3(b)(3) requires the broker to post collateral that fully secures the loan; collateral is cash or US Treasuries at 100-102% of loan value, marked to market daily. You are paid ONLY on shares actually out on loan, and only meaningfully on scarce ("special"/hard-to-borrow) names — general-collateral blue chips earn near zero. The catch is who holds the collateral: at Fidelity it sits at an independent custodial bank; at Schwab at Charles Schwab Trust Company (an affiliate); at IBKR the disclosure states the collateral "delivered to you by IB may constitute the only source of satisfaction of IB's obligation in the event that IB fails to return the securities" — i.e., you face IBKR directly.
evaluations.real_numbers: Verified Aug 2026: IBKR SYEP pays the client 50% of the borrow income and (uniquely) discloses the market rate; Fidelity/Schwab do not disclose the rate and pay less. Borrow-fee reality (S3 Partners / IBKR / Verdad data): general collateral ~0.30% annualized, and the most liquid names (SPY, AAPL, NVDA) borrow under ~1% — often a few basis points — so a diversified small holder of blue chips/ETFs earns almost nothing. Meaningful income comes only from hard-to-borrow "specials" at roughly 25-100%+ annualized; squeeze episodes spike far higher (GameStop's borrow fee went from ~1% in Jan 2019 to ~34% at the Jan 2021 squeeze; extreme cases exceed 1,000%). IBKR's own worked example: collateral of $375,000 x 4.5% = $16,875/yr — but that assumes a 4.5% (special) rate across a large balance; a typical retail holder rarely holds enough scarce names to realize that. Eligibility: IBKR requires a margin account or a cash account with liquid net worth > $25,000. Sources: interactivebrokers.com/en/pricing/stock-yield-enhancement-program.php; s3partners.com/articles/us-stock-borrow-fees; verdadcap.com/archive/costly-shorts.
evaluations.who_pays_you: The short seller pays the borrow fee. Structurally you are the "house" here, not the bettor — you own a scarce good (lendable shares of a hard-to-borrow name) and collect rent on that scarcity from someone who must pay to establish a short. This is the correct side of the FTD trade: the short bears locate cost, recall risk, negative carry and unbounded upside risk; you bear almost none of that. BUT the broker is an intermediary who keeps ~50%+ of the fee (IBKR discloses its 50/50 split; Fidelity/Schwab keep an undisclosed, larger cut), so you are the house minus a large management rake. The demand is rational and durable: shorts, market-makers hedging options/converts, and failed-delivery closers will always pay to borrow genuinely scarce stock.
evaluations.historical_failures: Documented, on-point retail harm — FINRA, Dec 2023: M1 Finance, Open to the Public (Public), SoFi Securities and SogoTrade were ordered to pay $2.6M ($1.6M fines + $1M+ restitution). The restitution specifically compensated retail customers whose shares were lent over a dividend record date and who suffered ADVERSE TAX CONSEQUENCES (dividends converted to ordinary-income payments-in-lieu). Individual restitution: M1 $736,917.86, SoFi $198,282.39, SogoTrade $104,767.25, Public $28,123. Customers had been auto-enrolled at account opening with no suitability screen. This is a concrete case where retail participants ended up NET-WORSE from lending. Broader securities-lending blow-ups (adjacent structure, not identical): AIG 2008 — its $80B sec-lending book required $58B+ of government assistance, but the loss came from reinvesting CASH COLLATERAL into RMBS, a reinvestment failure that does NOT occur in retail fully-paid lending (your collateral is held, not reinvested by you). Northern Trust 2008 took a $167.6M charge to backstop collateral-pool deficiencies; State Street and others had similar cash-collateral-pool losses, with some pension/401(k) lenders left on the hook (Forbes, "Securities Lending Meltdown," 2009). Lehman 2008: borrowed securities were not returned and lenders became unsecured creditors receiving fractions. These show the complex CAN blow up — but the specific fully-paid, non-reinvested, 100%-collateralized retail structure is materially safer than the agent-lending/reinvestment cases. No verified case exists of a large US retail broker (IBKR/Fidelity/Schwab) failing AND its fully-paid lenders losing principal net of collateral.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: Two things. (1) The tax trap dominating the fee: payments-in-lieu of dividends are taxed as ordinary income, losing qualified-dividend treatment (0/15/20% -> up to 37%). On a dividend-paying, LOW-fee name, the extra tax can exceed the borrow fee, turning the trade net-negative — the exact harm FINRA made four brokers pay restitution for. This is avoidable (lend only non-dividend hard-to-borrow names) but not everyone stays disciplined, and at Fidelity/Schwab you cannot pick which lots get lent or see the rate. (2) The correlated counterparty tail: your realized loss requires a "double default" — your broker fails AND the daily-marked collateral is simultaneously insufficient or frozen. The gap risk is largest precisely on the scarce, squeeze-prone names most worth lending (your lent name gaps +50% overnight while a broker heavily exposed to that same short crowd is under stress). Small probability but a genuine FAT, CORRELATED left tail. At IBKR the collateral is held by IBKR itself (not an independent custodian), concentrating that risk on one entity. Add loss of SIPC on the lent shares (replaced by collateral) and loss of voting rights during the loan.
evaluations.retail_accessible: Yes, genuinely — this is one of the few "be the lender" trades a small participant can actually execute. Enroll existing long holdings in IBKR SYEP (best transparency and a disclosed 50/50 split; needs a margin account or a cash account with >$25k liquid net worth), Fidelity Fully Paid Lending, or Schwab Fully Paid. No new capital, no new position risk — it is a toggle on shares you already hold. The practical limits: meaningful income requires holding hard-to-borrow names (themselves speculative), general-collateral holdings pay near zero, and you should restrict lending to non-dividend names to sidestep the QDI tax conversion. Prefer a broker that discloses the market rate (IBKR) so you can verify you are being paid fairly.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: Costs: the broker keeps roughly 50% (IBKR, disclosed) to substantially more (Fidelity/Schwab, undisclosed) of the borrow fee. Taxes: the killer detail. Any dividend paid while your shares are on loan reaches you as a "substitute payment in lieu of dividend," taxed as ORDINARY income — it is not a qualified dividend, so you lose the 0/15/20% preferential rate even though the underlying would have qualified (verified: IRS treatment, and the FINRA restitution was for exactly this). You also lose voting rights while on loan. Income is ordinary-rate regardless. Net effect: on a low-fee dividend payer the tax drag can exceed the fee; on a high-fee non-dividend special the fee dwarfs everything and the trade is cleanly positive. Discipline = lend the second kind, not the first.
evaluations.verdict: Strong but does NOT clear the 98% bar — I put it around 90%. This is the correct structural side (you are the house collecting scarcity rent, the short pays you, the carry is genuinely incremental on shares held anyway, and collateral is 100-102% marked daily), and for a truly disciplined participant who lends only non-dividend hard-to-borrow names through a transparent, well-capitalized broker (IBKR), long-term net-positive is very likely. Three things keep it under 98%: (1) documented retail NET-NEGATIVE outcomes already exist — FINRA forced $1M+ of restitution for the dividend/QDI tax conversion; (2) a fat, correlated counterparty double-default tail sits on exactly the squeeze-prone names most worth lending, with SIPC replaced by collateral you may have to chase in a bankruptcy; (3) fee compression means the typical small holder's general-collateral shares earn almost nothing, so the whole benefit hinges on holding — and correctly selecting — scarce names, which not every "disciplined" participant does. It is a good, largely-riskless incremental yield when executed with discipline, but "largely" is not "98% certain," so clears_98 = false.

evaluations.name: Risk-free rate: T-bills / money-market funds (the baseline)
evaluations.mechanics: You lend to the U.S. Treasury directly (buy a bill at a discount, redeem at par) or hold a government money-market fund / bill ETF (VMFXX, SPAXX, SGOV, BIL) that rolls very short Treasuries and repo. You get paid the accrued discount or a daily dividend. Return ~= the Fed's policy rate minus a small fee. There is no credit risk on direct Treasuries (full faith and credit) and near-zero credit risk on a government MMF; the only real variable is the level of short rates, which you do not control. This is not "a trade" in the edge-seeking sense — there is no risk premium being harvested and no counterparty being outsmarted. It is the price of deferring consumption, i.e. the benchmark against which every risk-bearing strategy must be judged.
evaluations.real_numbers: Verified as of Aug 12-13, 2026: 4-week T-bill ~3.69%; 3-month 3.81%; 6-month 3.93%; 12-month 4.00% (F/m Investments current-rates table, 08/12/2026; tradingeconomics 3-mo 3.80% on 08/13). VMFXX (Vanguard Federal MMF) 7-day SEC yield drifting ~3.7-4.2% (TTM 3.76%), expense ratio ~0.11%. Fed funds target 3.50-3.75%, held 9-3 at the July 29, 2026 FOMC. CPI +3.4% YoY, core CPI +2.5% (July 2026 report, released 08/12/2026). Implied real yield TODAY is slightly POSITIVE: ~+0.4% vs headline CPI, ~+1.3% vs core. This is a favorable-for-cash moment; it is not the historical norm.
evaluations.who_pays_you: The U.S. Treasury (ultimately the taxpayer) via the Fed's policy rate; for MMFs, the same plus short-term repo counterparties. Critically, they are NOT paying you a risk premium — they are paying you the pure time value of money for being the senior-most, first-in-line lender in the financial system. You are neither the house nor the bettor. You are the lender at the risk-free price, collecting rent on money itself. That is exactly why this is a benchmark and not an edge: nobody is transferring risk to you in exchange for expected profit.
evaluations.historical_failures: NOMINAL principal loss on direct T-bills held to maturity: none in modern U.S. history. The Treasury has never missed a bill payment; the 2011 S&P downgrade and repeated debt-ceiling standoffs (2011, 2013, 2023) caused zero missed payments — bills matured and paid at par. MONEY-MARKET FUNDS "breaking the buck" (the real, documented blow-ups): (1) Community Bankers U.S. Government Money Market Fund, Sept 1994 — the FIRST fund ever to break the buck; liquidated after losses on Federal Home Loan Bank / Sallie Mae structured-note derivatives during the 1994 rate spike; investors recovered ~96 cents on the dollar (an institutional fund). (2) Reserve Primary Fund, Sept 16, 2008 — $62.6B PRIME fund holding $785M of Lehman paper; NAV fell to ~$0.97, triggering a ~$300B+ run across prime MMFs; investors ultimately recovered ~99 cents after the Treasury's temporary money-fund guarantee. Both blow-ups were PRIME/credit or derivative funds — government MMFs and direct T-bills did not lose principal. Also note the NY Fed found ~28 additional funds would have broken the buck in 2008 absent sponsor bailouts (200+ voluntary sponsor rescues over the decades quietly absorbed losses). REAL (inflation-adjusted) losses — the true failure mode: 2021-2022 cash yielded ~0% while CPI peaked at 9.1% (June 2022), a real return near -8% in a single year; the 1970s stagflation produced multiple years of negative real bill returns; the 2010s ZIRP decade delivered persistently negative real yields. Long run (Dimson-Marsh-Staunton, 1900-2024), U.S. bills returned only ~+0.5%/yr in real terms GROSS — roughly zero to negative after tax for a taxable investor.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: Not default — inflation. The binding risk is a regime where the after-tax nominal yield sits below inflation for a stretch of years (ZIRP-plus-inflation, or 1970s-style stagflation), which makes the REAL, after-tax return negative even as the nominal balance keeps ticking up. A negative-NOMINAL-rate regime (never yet in the U.S., but real in the eurozone and Japan) combined with fees could even drive the nominal net return below zero; U.S. government funds have historically floored at ~0% by waiving fees, so a decade of negative nominal cumulative return is close to impossible. Fund-specific tail: a PRIME money fund holding commercial paper in a 2008-style run can break the buck for a ~1-4% loss — but this is fully avoidable by using a government MMF or holding bills directly, which is what a disciplined participant does.
evaluations.retail_accessible: Yes — the single most accessible position in all of finance. TreasuryDirect.gov buys bills directly with zero fee and a $100 minimum; any brokerage offers a government MMF (VMFXX, SPAXX, SNVXX) or a T-bill ETF (SGOV, BIL) with $0-$3,000 minimums, instant liquidity, and ~0.09-0.11% expense ratios. No accreditation, no capacity limit, no counterparty selection skill required.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: Costs are trivial (government MMF ER ~0.09-0.11%; direct bills free). Tax is the real erosion. Interest on T-bills and MMF dividends is taxed as ORDINARY income — up to 37% federal plus 3.8% NIIT — not the lower qualified-dividend/LTCG rate. Partial offset: T-bill interest is exempt from state and local tax (a genuine edge in high-tax states like CA/NY), and most government MMF dividends are partially state-exempt. Worked example at today's rates: a 3.8% yield at a 32% marginal federal rate nets ~2.6% after tax — already BELOW the 3.4% headline inflation rate, i.e. a negative real after-tax return even at this cycle's relatively high nominal yields. That is the crux: nominally positive with near-certainty, but really-and-after-tax it is frequently negative.
evaluations.verdict: This is the benchmark, not a trade — and it should be scored as such. On the bar AS WRITTEN (nominal, net-positive after costs and taxes over 10+ years), Treasuries and government MMFs clear 98% about as decisively as anything in finance can — call it 99.5%: the U.S. Treasury has never missed a bill payment, government MMFs have never broken the buck, U.S. nominal short rates have never gone negative, and fees are a rounding error against yield. So clears_98 = true. But be honest about what that near-certainty is: it is NOMINAL. On a REAL, after-tax basis the honest probability collapses toward a coin flip — 2021-22 alone cost cash ~8% of its real value in one year, the 1970s and the 2010s ZIRP decade delivered negative real yields, and the 125-year real return on bills is only ~+0.5%/yr gross, roughly zero after tax. Bottom line: it passes the stated test and is the correct risk-adjusted hurdle every other candidate must beat, but do NOT mistake "risk-free" for "loss-free." Its risk is inflation — real, recurring, and after-tax usually decisive — and it pays you no premium for bearing anything, because you are simply the senior lender collecting the price of money.

evaluations.name: Series I savings bonds / TIPS ladder (real-return floor)
evaluations.mechanics: You lend to the US Treasury and are paid an inflation adjustment (CPI-U) plus a contractually fixed real yield. Two instruments: (1) I-bonds: composite rate = fixed rate + semiannual inflation, reset every 6 months, floored at 0% (deflation can never make the composite negative). Fixed rate is locked for the bond's 30-yr life. Held to maturity/redemption, your pre-tax real return equals the fixed rate at purchase. (2) TIPS: principal is indexed to CPI-U; you receive a fixed real coupon on the adjusted principal, and at maturity you get the greater of adjusted principal or original par (deflation floor). Bought at a positive real yield and held to maturity, the pre-tax real return is contractually locked. Both are as close to a genuine risk-free real-return floor as exists for a small participant. This is a savings/allocation vehicle, not a trade — there is no spread to harvest and nothing to compound beyond the coupon.
evaluations.real_numbers: Verified Aug 2026. I-bond fixed rate 0.90%, composite 4.26% for bonds issued May 1–Oct 31 2026 (prior period composite 4.03%); composite floored at 0% — source TreasuryDirect i-bonds-interest-rates page and tipswatch 2026-04-30, corroborated by CNBC 2026-04-30. TIPS real yields ~2.31% at 10yr and ~2.87% at 30yr as of the July 17 2026 Treasury Daily Real Yield Curve (TheStreet, 2026), well above the ~0.9% 10-yr historical average. Purchase cap: $10,000/yr electronic per SSN via TreasuryDirect; the $5,000 paper-I-bond-via-tax-refund route was eliminated Jan 1 2025 (tipswatch 2024-09-01; Kiplinger). Redemption rules: no redemption in first 12 months; 3-month interest penalty if redeemed before 5 years; penalty-free after 5 yrs (31 CFR 359.7; TreasuryDirect). Costs: essentially $0 at TreasuryDirect/auction; TIPS fund expense ratios ~0.03%–0.20% (e.g. Schwab/Vanguard TIPS funds). Dollars: $10k I-bond at today's 0.90% fixed ≈ $90/yr of guaranteed real purchasing power above inflation; a $10k 10-yr TIPS at +2.3% real ≈ $230/yr real, pre-tax.
evaluations.who_pays_you: Counterparty is the US Treasury (full-faith-and-credit). You are neither the house nor the bettor — you are a lender receiving a defined inflation+real coupon. The Treasury pays because it needs to borrow and is willing to sell inflation insurance; you are effectively buying that insurance at whatever real yield the auction sets. It is a rational, non-adversarial exchange: you accept a low but near-certain real return in exchange for the government bearing inflation risk. There is no counterparty being outsmarted, so the return is capped at the offered real yield — you cannot earn an edge, only lock a floor.
evaluations.historical_failures: Held-to-maturity individual securities have essentially never lost in pre-tax REAL terms, but there are well-documented losses in adjacent, realistic forms: (1) 2022 — the Bloomberg US TIPS Index posted roughly -12% total return (average index price fell ~19%) as real yields jumped ~250+ bps; TIPS FUND holders and anyone who sold before maturity took large nominal AND real losses (Morningstar, 'Why Are Inflation-Protected Bond Funds Losing Money'). (2) 2013 taper tantrum — TIPS funds fell sharply for the same reason. (3) 0%-fixed-rate I-bond vintages — I-bonds issued Nov 2010, May 2020–Nov 2021, and much of 2008–2019 carried a 0.00% fixed rate, so their held-to-maturity real return is exactly 0% pre-tax and NEGATIVE after federal tax on the inflation compensation (My Money Blog; TreasuryDirect fixed-rate history). (4) After-tax real losses in high inflation — because federal tax is levied on the full nominal return (I-bond interest at redemption; TIPS 'phantom income' on principal adjustments annually, even though not received until maturity), a high-inflation decade in a taxable account can produce a negative after-tax real return even on a positively-yielding bond (tipswatch TIPS In-Depth; Morningstar). So the disqualifying cases are real: fund/early-sale drawdowns, 0%-fixed vintages, and after-tax real erosion under high inflation.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: Three mechanisms. (1) Phantom-income/inflation tax in a TAXABLE account: federal tax hits the nominal return including the inflation compensation, so a sustained high-inflation decade (a 1970s or even 2021-23 repeat) can push the AFTER-TAX real return negative even at a positive stated real yield — and 10+ years is long enough that we cannot assign a high-inflation regime a probability below 2%. (2) Selling before maturity into a real-yield spike (2013, 2022) converts the 'floor' into a realized real loss — this defeats fund holders and anyone needing liquidity, and is a behavioral trap. (3) Low/zero fixed-rate entry: a buyer of a 0%-fixed I-bond earns 0% real pre-tax, negative after tax. Add CPI-methodology/basis risk (your personal inflation may exceed CPI-U) and the $10k/yr I-bond cap, which prevents it from ever being a standalone wealth strategy.
evaluations.retail_accessible: Yes, fully — this is a genuinely retail-native vehicle. I-bonds: buy directly at TreasuryDirect.gov, $10k/yr per SSN (couples $20k; trusts/entities can stack additional accounts). TIPS: buy at Treasury auction commission-free via TreasuryDirect or any brokerage, build a maturity ladder, or hold a low-cost TIPS fund/ETF (~0.03%–0.20% ER). The strongest, near-98% version is a TIPS ladder held to maturity INSIDE a tax-advantaged account (IRA), which eliminates the annual phantom-income tax drag — that specific implementation is close to a true locked positive real return. The taxable-account, generic implementation is what falls short of the bar.
evaluations.verdict: One of the strongest capital-preservation candidates assessed, but it does not clear the 98% REAL-after-tax bar as a general strategy for a small participant. Nominal net-positive if held to maturity is near-certain (~99.5%); the gap is entirely after-tax REAL. The phantom-income tax on inflation compensation means a high-inflation decade in a taxable account can produce a negative after-tax real return, and 10+ years is long enough that such a regime cannot be ruled out at 98% confidence; historical 0%-fixed I-bond vintages and the 2022/2013 fund drawdowns are concrete evidence of the failure modes. Calibrated at ~92%: excellent real-return floor and the closest thing to risk-free that a small saver can buy, but capacity-capped ($10k/yr I-bonds), behaviorally dependent on holding to maturity, and tax-exposed enough that I would not defend >=98% real-positive. Best used as an inflation-hedged safe-asset allocation — ideally TIPS in a tax-advantaged account — not as a return-generating trade.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: I-bond interest is federal-taxable but exempt from state/local tax; tax is deferred until redemption/maturity (up to 30 yrs) and can be fully tax-free if used for qualified higher education (income-limited) — these are genuine advantages. TIPS are federal-taxable on both coupons AND the annual inflation adjustment to principal ('phantom income') even though that adjustment is not received until maturity, and are also state/local exempt. The erosion: because tax is assessed on the NOMINAL return (real yield + inflation compensation), the effective tax rate on the real return rises as inflation rises. At a 24% federal marginal rate and 4% inflation, tax alone can consume ~1%+ of return — enough to flip a +0.9% real yield to negative after-tax real. Explicit costs are trivial: $0 at TreasuryDirect/auction, ~3–20 bps for funds. The tax drag, not fees, is the binding cost and the main reason the after-tax real return is not reliably positive in taxable accounts during high inflation.

evaluations.name: Cash-and-carry / delta-neutral funding-rate capture (equity index and crypto)
evaluations.mechanics: Two very different trades bundled under one label. (A) EQUITY INDEX: buy the index (ETF/basket), short the future. The future embeds price x (risk-free r - dividend yield q + a financing/convenience spread). Long-spot/short-future harvests roughly risk-free + that spread; it is a cash-enhancement, not an independent edge. (B) CRYPTO: hold spot (or a long-dated future) and short the perpetual, or run any spot-long/perp-short delta-neutral pair, collecting the funding rate that longs pay shorts (and/or the calendar basis). You are delta-neutral on price and get paid the carry/funding for as long as it stays positive net of fees. Critically, the crypto short leg REQUIRES posting collateral on a centralized venue, so the payoff is 'small positive carry most of the time, occasional total loss of venue collateral' — a short-volatility profile, not a free lunch.
evaluations.real_numbers: CRYPTO (verified, secondary sources): BTC 3-month annualized futures basis has compressed to ~2-3% as of 8 Aug 2026 (down from ~20% in the 2021 bull market; ~3.8% in Feb 2026). CME carry read 5.69-7.89% on some Aug-2026 contracts by one methodology but ~3% by another — sources conflict. Decisively, BTC's 3-month basis has paid LESS than the 2-year U.S. Treasury (~3.8-4.19%) every month since Feb 2026 — 'only the second time on record.' So current excess return over risk-free T-bills is negative. Ethena (largest live delta-neutral funding product) reports realized APY ~4-30% across 2024-25, but ~17.5% of days over ~3 years had negative summed ETH funding, longest negative streak 13 days. EQUITY INDEX (CME Group): S&P 500 futures implied financing spread/convenience yield ranged 0-110 bps, averaging 35.5 bps, Feb 2024-Mar 2025 — i.e. long-spot/short-future earns roughly risk-free + ~0.35%, barely above just holding T-bills. FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED: the '8-20% APY,' '19.26% return / <2% drawdown,' 'up to 115.9% in six months' figures come from promotional arbitrage-tool affiliate blogs and are cherry-picked good-regime marketing, not audited track records.
evaluations.who_pays_you: CRYPTO FUNDING: leveraged directional longs (bulls using perps to get levered exposure) pay funding to shorts in bull/greedy regimes — so you are 'the house' selling leverage to over-eager longs, but ONLY while sentiment is long-skewed; when the crowd flips short (bear markets, 2022), funding goes negative and you become the payer. You are NOT structurally the house — you rent out balance sheet to whichever side is crowded, and the sign flips. EQUITY INDEX: you are paid by participants who want cheap synthetic leverage via futures and by the balance-sheet scarcity premium (dealers charge a spread for financing the index); this spread is a genuine but tiny 'you-are-the-house' premium (~35 bps) over risk-free. In both cases the counterparty rationally pays you a modest premium for providing leverage/liquidity — but the venue/clearer sits between you and that payment, and in crypto the venue itself is the real risk.
evaluations.historical_failures: Multiple documented, full-loss blow-ups. (1) GBTC BASIS-TRADE COLLAPSE 2021-22: the canonical crypto cash-and-carry (deposit BTC -> receive GBTC shares trading at up to ~120% premium -> sell) reversed to a deep discount (>40%) as competition/ETF hopes shifted; Three Arrows Capital (largest GBTC holder, ~$1B position), BlockFi, Genesis, Celsius and Voyager all went bankrupt, many using leverage on the 'arb.' (2) FTX, Nov 2022: traders running delta-neutral funding capture with collateral or a leg on FTX lost it entirely the moment the venue failed (~$8B customer shortfall) — being market-neutral gave zero protection because the venue vaporized the collateral. FTX creditors eventually got ~118% in USD, but only after ~2.5 years and paid in depressed Nov-2022 dollars (crypto multiplied several-fold since, so holders were badly worse off). (3) Nov 2022 / 2022 bear generally: perpetual funding turned persistently negative (~-0.01%/8h for BTCUSDT) and basis collapsed, turning the 'carry' into a cost. (4) Broader venue-failure base rate: QuadrigaCX (2019, ~13% recovered), Mt Gox (850k BTC lost, ~a decade to partial repayment), Celsius/Voyager/BlockFi freezes, Gemini Earn/Genesis freeze — a 10-year horizon in crypto almost always contains at least one catastrophic venue event, and this strategy structurally forces you onto a venue.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: The fat left tail is CENTRALIZED-VENUE FAILURE while you hold collateral there — a full-capital-loss event, not a drawdown, and unavoidable because the short leg must be margined on a venue. FTX (a Sequoia/BlackRock-backed 'adult in the room') failing proves 'use only reputable venues' does not eliminate it. Second: FUNDING/BASIS REGIME FLIP — the carry is short-vol; it is negative in bear markets (2022) and, as of 2026, has compressed below T-bills, so you can earn nothing (or pay) for extended stretches while still carrying the tail. Third: LIQUIDATION OF THE PERP LEG on a violent move (even at low leverage) forces you to close the short at the worst price and leaves you naked long. Fourth: withdrawal freezes / de-pegging of the stablecoin collateral. Any one of these can make a disciplined participant net-negative over a decade.
evaluations.retail_accessible: Partly. EQUITY INDEX version is accessible (ETF + CME/micro futures, regulated, cleared) but the ~35 bps edge over T-bills is eaten by quarterly roll costs, bid/ask, margin management and dividend-forecast risk, so for a small participant it is dominated by simply holding T-bills/a money-market fund — a complicated way to earn cash returns, not a real edge. CRYPTO version is accessible on major exchanges (spot + perp, or spot + dated future) and via products like Ethena's sUSDe, but requires 24/7 monitoring, active management of a sign-flipping funding rate, unavoidable venue custody exposure, and — critically right now — offers negative excess return over T-bills after compression. A disciplined small participant CAN run it, but cannot obtain the institutional custody, insurance, venue diversification and monitoring that would meaningfully cap the tail.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: Heavy drag. CRYPTO: funding receipts and perp gains are ordinary income / short-term in the U.S. (crypto perps are not Section 1256; funding is taxed as ordinary income as received), so a large share of an already-thin, volatile carry is taxed at the top marginal rate; frequent rebalancing generates constant taxable events and wash-sale ambiguity. Trading fees, funding-settlement slippage, and the spot/perp bid-ask on every rebalance compound the erosion, and the ~0.007%/8h Binance break-even fee threshold means low-funding regimes net to zero or negative. EQUITY INDEX: broad-based index futures do get favorable 60/40 Section 1256 treatment, but on a ~35 bps gross spread the after-tax, after-roll-cost residual is negligible for retail. Net: taxes and costs convert a low-single-digit gross carry into something at or below a plain T-bill for most small participants.
evaluations.verdict: FAILS the 98% bar decisively. This is 'near-arbitrage when it exists' — and both halves are compromised for a small participant. The equity-index leg is nearly riskless but nearly return-less (dominated by just buying T-bills). The crypto leg is where the yield historically lived, but it carries a documented, non-diversifiable fat left tail: the strategy structurally forces collateral onto a centralized venue, and the last decade is littered with full-loss venue failures (FTX, Celsius, Voyager, QuadrigaCX, Mt Gox) plus a canonical basis-trade wipeout (GBTC/3AC/BlockFi/Genesis, 2021-22). On top of the tail, the carry is short-vol and regime-dependent (persistently negative in 2022) and is presently COMPRESSED BELOW T-BILLS (every month since Feb 2026), so the current excess return over the risk-free alternative is negative while the tail remains. After ordinary-income taxes and rebalancing costs, a disciplined small participant is realistically net-positive over 10+ years perhaps ~60% of the time — better than a coin flip because funding is positive most of the time and a stop-when-uneconomic discipline helps, but nowhere near 98%. The whole point of '98%' is the absence of a documented blow-up and a durable edge; this strategy has multiple documented blow-ups and a currently-negative edge. Do not certify.

evaluations.name: Premium selling: covered calls / cash-secured puts / buy-write indices (BXM, PUT)
evaluations.mechanics: You sell optionality and collect the premium. Covered call = own the underlying + sell a call against it (cap upside, keep the premium). Cash-secured put = hold cash + sell a put (get paid to agree to buy the underlying lower; economically identical payoff to a covered call at the same strike). Buy-write indices (CBOE BXM = S&P 500 + monthly ATM call write; PUT = collateralized monthly ATM put write) systematize this. You get paid because implied volatility trades, on average, above subsequently realized volatility — the variance risk premium (VRP). In the FULLY COLLATERALIZED form the payoff = long-equity beta MINUS the capped upside PLUS the premium: a negatively skewed return with a BOUNDED left tail (worst case = the underlying's own drawdown minus premium, not a wipeout). The critical fork: collateralized (BXM/PUT/covered calls/CSPs) survives the tail and merely underperforms; NAKED or LEVERAGED short-vol (XIV, SVXY, short strangles, ODTE, the LJM/Allianz funds) has an UNBOUNDED left tail and periodically goes to zero. The candidate as scoped is the collateralized version; my probability is anchored there.
evaluations.real_numbers: Verified this session. LONG-RUN COLLATERALIZED PERFORMANCE: BXM (buy-write) 1988-2006 returned 11.77%/yr vs S&P 500 11.67%/yr, at 9.29% vol vs 13.89% — roughly the same return at ~2/3 the risk. Over June 1986-Jan 2012, $1 grew to $9.43 in BXM vs $9.44 in the S&P — essentially identical for 25+ years (HewittEnnisKnupp/Cboe). PUT (put-write) Jul 1986-Oct 2008 returned 10.32%/yr vs S&P 8.77%/yr, vol 9.91% vs 15.39%, max drawdown -32.7% vs -50.9% (Ennis Knupp/Cboe). So collateralized index buy-write has historically been net-positive across every US decade in the sample, including ones containing 2000-02, 2008, and 2020. THE CATCH (capped upside): in the 2010s bull run the strategy badly lagged. QYLD (Global X Nasdaq-100 covered call): NAV eroded ~35% over the decade to ~2026 while total return was +155% vs QQQ +572%; a $10k position from 2014 paid ~$14k of distributions but the stake is worth ~$6.5k, and recent distributions were partly return of capital (Yahoo/24-7 Wall St). Sources: spglobal.com SPDJI research; Cboe BXM/PUT factsheets and HewittEnnisKnupp (2012) and Ennis Knupp PUT study; en.wikipedia.org CBOE BuyWrite/PutWrite; finance.yahoo.com QYLD.
evaluations.who_pays_you: You are the house — mostly. The counterparties are call buyers (paying for leveraged upside/lottery convexity) and put buyers (paying for downside insurance). They rationally overpay because both crave the convex, limited-loss payoff you are short; that persistent overpayment is the variance risk premium — implied vol has averaged above realized vol, so the seller has a small real structural edge. BUT you are the house running an insurance book with a fat claims tail: many small premiums collected, then an occasional large payout when the underlying gaps against you. Collateralized, you can pay the claim (you just book a bad year and give up the rebound); naked/leveraged, one claim exceeds your capital and you are insolvent. So: you are the house on the collateralized book, but the edge is thin, the skew is negative, and the same trade done on margin turns you into a bettor who eventually meets the tail.
evaluations.historical_failures: All verified this session. (1) XIV (VelocityShares Daily Inverse VIX ETN): Feb 5, 2018 "Volmageddon" — VIX 17.31 to 37.32 — inverse-vol ETPs lost ~$3B in ~50 minutes; XIV fell ~97% (indicative value to ~$4) and Credit Suisse terminated it (last trade Feb 15, 2018). Leveraged/uncollateralized short-vol, NOT a covered call — the definitive naked-vol blow-up. (2) LJM PRESERVATION AND GROWTH FUND (LJMIX) — a RETAIL mutual fund literally named "Preservation": sold uncovered S&P options, lost >80% Feb 2-7, 2018 ($812M to $14M), liquidated March 2018; FINRA fined the distributors. Retail could and did buy this. (3) Allianz Structured Alpha: an options-selling strategy sold to 114 institutions (pension funds for teachers, clergy, bus drivers); ~$7B of losses in the March 2020 crash; AGI US pled guilty to criminal securities fraud, sentenced to >$463M forfeiture + >$3.23B restitution + >$2.33B fines, plus >$5B civil settlements. (4) QYLD: not a wipeout but a documented retail failure of naive systematic ATM covered-call writing — ~35% NAV erosion over a decade while the underlying tripled, i.e. the capped-upside/full-downside asymmetry compounding against holders. COUNTERPOINT the bull case leans on: the COLLATERALIZED index versions (BXM, PUT) have NO 10-year net-negative window in the ~35-year US sample — but the sample is short, overlapping, single-country, and a Nikkei buy-write from 1989 would have been deeply negative for well over a decade.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: Four things, in descending relevance to the collateralized version. (1) FULL EQUITY BETA WITH A CAPPED RECOVERY. Buy-write eats nearly the whole drawdown in a deep crash (a 1-2% monthly premium barely cushions a 30-50% fall) but then CAPS the rebound by re-writing calls into the recovery. A 10-year window that opens near a top with a deep crash followed by a strong-but-capped recovery can be net-negative — QYLD's ~35% NAV erosion is that mechanism running live. (2) SECULAR BEAR / REGIME RISK. The strategy inherits equity's own 10-year downside; equity has had ~flat-to-negative real decades (US 2000-2009; Japan post-1989 for 20+ years), and buy-write cannot escape a market that simply does not recover. (3) TAX DRAG (taxable accounts): premium and CSP income are short-term capital gains, and constant monthly realization plus straddle-rule loss deferral erode the thin VRP edge — enough to flip marginal decades negative. (4) DISCIPLINE DECAY — the dominant real-world failure. "Selling vol for income" is a slippery category: chasing yield pushes retail into single-name concentration, ATM over-writing (QYLD), or naked/leveraged short-vol (XIV, LJM, Allianz), where the left tail becomes unbounded and ruin is eventually near-certain. The 98% bar assumes the participant never once drifts across that line over 10+ years; that assumption is itself unlikely.
evaluations.retail_accessible: Yes, very — and that accessibility is part of the hazard. A small participant can sell cash-secured puts or covered calls on liquid index ETFs (SPY/QQQ) directly, or buy packaged funds: BXMX/PBP (S&P buy-write), XYLD, QYLD, or JEPI/JEPQ (active covered-call). Execution is easy; executing WELL is not. The most-marketed retail products (QYLD's headline "~12% yield") are exactly the NAV-eroding at-the-money over-writers, and the naked version that wiped out 80% (LJM) was a retail-available mutual fund. So retail can do the sound collateralized version, but the retail funnel actively steers toward the eroding and blow-up variants.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: Costs: option bid-ask spreads plus per-contract commissions on monthly rolls; manageable on liquid SPX/SPY options but a steady leak that directly nets against a thin VRP edge. Assignment/early-exercise and roll mistiming add slippage. Taxes (taxable accounts, the bigger erosion): covered-call premium and ALL cash-secured-put income are taxed as SHORT-TERM capital gains (ordinary rates); frequent monthly realization forfeits the tax deferral that is a core advantage of equity buy-and-hold; in-the-money/"unqualified" covered calls can suspend the stock's holding period and convert a long-term gain into short-term; and straddle rules defer losses against unrecognized gains. Packaged funds (QYLD) partly mask this by paying return-of-capital distributions — tax-deferred, but it is your own principal handed back, not yield. Net effect: in a taxable account the after-tax edge is materially thinner than the pre-tax BXM/PUT backtests imply; in an IRA/401(k) the strategy is much more defensible.
evaluations.verdict: FAILS the 98% bar — calibrated ~87% net-positive over 10+ years for a DISCIPLINED small participant running the COLLATERALIZED version (covered calls / CSPs / BXM-PUT-style buy-write) on a broad liquid index in a tax-advantaged account. This is a genuinely reasonable, positive-expectancy strategy: it monetizes a real and persistent variance risk premium, has matched the S&P's long-run return at ~2/3 the volatility (BXM 11.77% vs 11.67%; PUT 10.32% vs 8.77% with a -32.7% vs -50.9% max drawdown), and — unlike naked short-vol — has a BOUNDED left tail that has stayed net-positive across every US decade in the sample. That is why it scores well above a coin flip. But three structural facts keep it far from 98%: (a) it carries full equity-market regime risk (a lost decade or a Japan-style secular bear drags it negative — no VRP saves you if the underlying never recovers); (b) the capped-upside/full-downside asymmetry means a deep-crash-then-strong-recovery decade can leave even the collateralized version net-negative, with QYLD's ~35% NAV erosion as the live demonstration; and (c) the after-tax edge in a taxable account is thin enough to flip marginal windows. Above all, "selling volatility for income" is a category with a documented graveyard — XIV (-97%, terminated), LJM Preservation & Growth (-80%, a retail fund, liquidated), Allianz Structured Alpha (~$7B, criminal fraud plea) — and the retail funnel steers toward exactly those eroding/leveraged variants. A 98% claim would require certainty that the participant never drifts across the collateralized line and never meets a bad-sequence decade; neither is defensible. Net-positive: probably. 98% certain: no.

evaluations.name: Diversified Merger Arbitrage
evaluations.mechanics: Buy the target of an announced deal below the agreed takeout price; the gap ("deal spread") converges to the deal price at closing. Cash deals = own the target; stock deals = long target / short acquirer to lock the exchange ratio. Diversified across many simultaneous live deals so no single break is fatal. You are paid the residual completion risk premium: on average you earn a few percent on deals that close and take a larger loss on the minority that break. Verdad's 2000-2020 study of 835 deals: +2.0% on completed deals, -2.8% on cancelled deals, ~89% completion rate, blended ~1.5% gross per deal (annualized higher because deals close in months). Structurally a short-volatility / insurance-selling carry trade, not a true riskless arbitrage.
evaluations.real_numbers: VERIFIED. Index level (HFRI ED: Merger Arbitrage, inception Dec 1989): a fund-manager source (Accelerate/Klymochko, PROMOTIONAL — flag) cites ~7.4% annualized, "only two down years since inception," 2nd-highest Sharpe of 40 HFRI strategies, 5th-smallest max drawdown. More neutral: 2009-2019 ~4.1% annualized, 2.5% std dev, Sharpe ~1.64. 2025 YTD (through Sept): HFRI ED Merger Arb +8.2%, strongest since 2021. Retail vehicles: MERFX (The Merger Fund, since 1989) ~4.2% annualized since inception, POSITIVE IN 33 OF 37 YEARS, worst year 2008 = -2.26%; expense ratio net ~0.95-1.56% (gross 1.67%) by share class. MNA (NYLI/IQ Merger Arbitrage ETF, launched Nov 2009): expense 0.77%, ~2.71% annualized since inception, ~3.12% over 10yr (vs S&P ~12.97%). Current spreads (2025): median gross spread ~5.9% across ~1,700 historical observations; elevated portfolios cited near 9-11% in the current wide-spread environment. Academic anchor: Mitchell & Pulvino (J. Finance 2001, 4,750 mergers 1963-1998) ~4% excess return/yr after transaction costs.
evaluations.who_pays_you: The target's existing shareholders, who sell you the stock below the takeout price because they want certainty and liquidity NOW rather than wait months bearing deal-break risk. You are the HOUSE selling completion insurance — positive expected value because ~89-95% of announced deals close. But it is a house that resembles a short-put writer: the acquirer, financing banks, and antitrust/foreign regulators are the parties who can blow up the trade, and your worst losses cluster exactly when many deals break at once (recessions, credit freezes, hostile antitrust regimes). So you are the house on average but the bettor in the tail.
evaluations.historical_failures: VERIFIED cases where it lost money. (1) 2007-08 credit-crisis LBO break cluster: Sallie Mae/SLM (J.C. Flowers consortium walked, Dec 2007), Harman/KKR-Goldman (Sept 2007), Alliance Data/Blackstone, plus the "arbitrage crash" (Mitchell & Pulvino 2012) — levered risk-arb funds forced to deleverage as spreads blew out in Q4 2008. Diversified UNLEVERED funds only mildly hurt: MERFX 2008 -2.26%, HFRI merger arb down modestly. Levered players suffered far worse. (2) 2016 antitrust/inversion cluster: Pfizer/Allergan ~$160bn killed Apr 2016 by US Treasury inversion rules; Halliburton/Baker Hughes abandoned May 2016 (DOJ, $3.5bn break fee); Staples/Office Depot blocked May 2016. (3) 2018 Qualcomm/NXP $44bn terminated Jul 2018 — China's SAMR withheld approval amid the US-China trade war (the "China" break; $2bn termination fee). (4) 2020 COVID: March spread blowout; deals renegotiated lower or terminated — Tiffany/LVMH cut $135->$131.50, L Brands/Sycamore terminated, Simon Property/Taubman renegotiated down. (5) 2021-22 Khan (FTC)/Kanter (DOJ) record enforcement — most merger challenges since the 1976 HSR Act: Nvidia/Arm and Lockheed/Aerojet Rocketdyne both terminated Feb 2022, Penguin RH/Simon & Schuster blocked, Twitter/Musk near-break (Musk tried to walk Jul 2022, spread widened to ~30%+ before closing Oct 2022); some large open-ended arb funds sharply trailed benchmarks. KEY PATTERN: catastrophic losses concentrate in LEVERED or UNDIVERSIFIED books; the diversified unlevered index/funds have no negative 10-year window on record and a worst annual loss in the low single digits.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: The genuine fat left tail — the payoff is empirically that of SELLING UNCOVERED INDEX PUTS (Mitchell & Pulvino 2001): returns are positively correlated with the market only in severely depreciating markets, so the strategy loses precisely when equities crash and deals break en masse. The historical sample has never contained a truly systemic multi-year break wave (a prolonged LBO-financing freeze plus a regime that blocks a large fraction of deals for years) — that scenario is under-sampled, not impossible. Combined with (a) secular spread compression from crowding (net returns fell to ~2-3% post-2009, e.g. MNA 2.71%), (b) fees of 0.77%-1.7%, and (c) short-term/ordinary-income tax on nearly all gains, the forward net-of-fee-and-tax margin is thin enough that a compressed-spread decade plus one bad break cluster could push a specific 10-year window to marginally negative. Capacity is also limited: returns shrink as capital floods in.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: The biggest structural leak. Deals close in months, so essentially ALL gains are short-term / ordinary income taxed up to 37% federal + state (no long-term capital-gains treatment, no qualified-dividend break). On a ~3-4% gross post-compression return, that alone can remove ~1.0-1.4 points. Fees stack on top: 0.77% for the cheapest ETF (MNA), ~0.95-1.7% for active mutual funds (MERFX). Realistic taxable small-participant math: ~3.5% gross - ~0.8-1.5% fees - ~35% tax on the remainder ≈ ~1.5-2.0% net nominal in a normal decade, and thinner if spreads stay compressed. Best held in a tax-deferred account, where the tax drag disappears and net-positive-over-10-years confidence rises materially.
evaluations.retail_accessible: Yes, easily and this is a strength. Passive/low-cost: MNA (NYLI Merger Arbitrage ETF, 0.77%) tracks a diversified merger-arb index. Active mutual funds: MERFX/MERIX (The Merger Fund, since 1989), plus BALPX, ARBFX/ARBNX (Water Island). These provide instant diversification across dozens of live deals with no leverage. Doing it yourself deal-by-deal is possible but dangerous for a small participant: single-deal concentration reproduces the blow-up cases above, spreads are thin so mistakes are costly, and short legs on stock deals add operational friction. The disciplined small-participant version is a diversified fund/ETF, ideally in a tax-sheltered account.
evaluations.verdict: HIGH probability but does NOT clear 98%. Diversified, unlevered merger arbitrage is one of the most consistent strategies in existence — MERFX positive in 33 of 37 years with a worst year of -2.26%; the HFRI index has among the smallest drawdowns and no negative 10-year window on record; you are structurally the house collecting a completion-risk premium. That empirical record argues for a very high net-positive probability. But three things keep it below the 98% bar: (1) the payoff is genuinely a short-put with an under-sampled catastrophic left tail that hits exactly in systemic break waves; (2) secular spread compression and capacity limits have thinned net returns to ~2-3%; and (3) short-term/ordinary-income taxation plus fees can erode that thin margin toward zero, so a compressed-spread decade plus a bad break cluster could plausibly (>2% chance) leave a taxable small participant marginally negative over a given 10-year window. I calibrate ~90% net-positive after costs and taxes (higher, ~94-95%, if held tax-deferred). Robust and defensible, but not a 98% near-certainty.

evaluations.name: Liquidity provision / rebate capture / AMM LP
evaluations.mechanics: You post resting orders or deposit assets into a pool and are paid a fee/rebate every time someone trades against you. Gross income = maker rebate (equities/CEX) or swap fees pro-rata to your share (AMM). Against that you net: (1) adverse selection — the trades that hit you are disproportionately from informed counterparties (arbitrageurs, HFT) who trade precisely when your price is stale, so you systematically buy what's falling and sell what's rising; (2) in AMMs this is formalized as LVR (loss-versus-rebalancing) and its realized cousin impermanent loss; (3) infrastructure/gas; (4) smart-contract, depeg, and venue risk; (5) taxes. You are net-positive only if fees earned exceed adverse selection + costs. The structural problem: the people who pay you the most (informed flow) also take the most from you, and a small participant has no way to accept only the uninformed flow (wholesalers buy that via PFOF).
evaluations.real_numbers: VERIFIED. AMM LP: Topaze Blue/Bancor study of Uniswap v3 (Loesch, Hindman, Richardson, Welch, Nov 2021) — 17,000+ wallets, 17 pools (~43% of TVL), 5 months: $199M fees vs $260M+ impermanent loss; 49.5% of LPs had NEGATIVE returns vs simply holding; per-pool negative shares USDC/ETH 62%, MKR/ETH 74%; no profitability edge from active vs passive management; only automated JIT bots consistently beat buy-and-hold (cryptobriefing.com, nasdaq.com). LVR: closed-form σ²/8 adverse-selection drain (Milionis-Moallemi-Roughgarden-Zhang 2022; a16zcrypto.com) — an ETH-USDC pool at 5% daily vol loses ~3.125 bps/day ≈ ~11%/yr to arbitrageurs BEFORE fees. Equity maker rebate cap = $0.0030/share (30 mils), being lowered by SEC's Oct-2024 Reg NMS amendments (sidley.com, sec.gov); primary beneficiaries are professional market makers, and retail marketable flow is routed via PFOF while retail resting-order rebates are typically kept by the broker/exchange net-capture. Crypto CEX: Binance retail spot maker fee is a POSITIVE 0.10% (a cost); negative-fee/market-maker rebate programs require ~$10M–$20M+ monthly volume plus large BNB holdings (binance.com, support.binance.us) — inaccessible to a small participant. Gas: entering an Ethereum Uniswap LP position >$12, swaps $5–30 (atise.medium.com); small LPs structurally disadvantaged and pushed to high-fee pools. Stablecoin/correlated pools: quoted 3–10%+ APY, but frequently boosted by CRV-style token emissions (a subsidy, not organic fee income).
evaluations.who_pays_you: Traders who take liquidity pay the fee/rebate. But the payer pool is bifurcated: uninformed/noise traders pay you and you keep it (you are the house); informed traders (arbitrageurs, HFT, MEV searchers) pay the same fee but extract more than it via stale-price adverse selection (they are the sharks and YOU are the bettor). Rationally they pay because the fee is smaller than the mispricing they capture. In an open venue a small participant cannot segment out the informed flow — wholesalers already buy the clean retail flow through PFOF, and AMMs are permissionlessly open to every arbitrage bot. So on average, in accessible venues, you are the bettor against informed flow, not the house — unless you personally have a speed or information edge, which a small disciplined participant does not.
evaluations.historical_failures: Well documented. (1) Uniswap v3, 2021 — ~half of all LPs (49.5%) underperformed holding; some pools 62–74% negative (Topaze Blue/Bancor). (2) Terra/UST depeg, May 2022 — AMM/Curve LPs were left holding the collapsing UST leg as arbitrageurs drained the good assets; ~$60B ecosystem wipeout (calebandbrown.com, elliptic via chainkraft). (3) USDC depeg, Mar 2023 — Curve 3pool composition swung from ~33% to ~83% USDC in hours as informed traders dumped USDC onto LPs; LPs earned ~$4.9M fees that week but were left holding the depegged asset and were rescued only by the FDIC-driven repeg — the adverse-selection tail was realized and survival was luck, not skill (xenophonlabs.substack.com, eigenphi). (4) Curve Vyper reentrancy exploit, Jul 30 2023 — malformed compiler locks let attackers drain multiple pools; ~$52–70M lost, LP principal stolen (chainalysis.com, halborn.com). Beyond these, routine AMM pool exploits and token rugs recur. Equity/CEX maker-rebate 'failures' for retail are structural rather than event-driven: retail simply cannot access the rebate, so there is nothing to blow up — the strategy is unavailable, not merely risky.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: Structural adverse selection (LVR) is a permanent, mathematically guaranteed drag that grows with volatility, and a passive small LP has no offsetting edge. Fee compression: as capital chases attractive pools, per-LP fee yield falls toward the LVR line. Capacity/subsidy decay: the 'safe' stablecoin-pool returns lean heavily on token emissions that are unsustainable and shrinking. Fat left tail on the accessible form (AMM LP): stablecoin depeg (UST, USDC) can leave you holding the worthless leg, and smart-contract exploits (Curve Vyper) can take principal outright — over a 10+ year horizon the cumulative probability of hitting at least one such event is material. Gas/fixed costs make small positions uneconomic on L1. For the maker-rebate form, the strategy is simply inaccessible to retail (brokers/HFT capture the rebate; retail pays maker fees or sells flow via PFOF).
evaluations.retail_accessible: Partially, and only in its worst-EV form. Equity maker rebates: effectively NOT accessible — retail resting-order rebates are captured by the broker/exchange and marketable flow is sold via PFOF; the payers of rebates are professional market makers. Crypto CEX maker rebates: NOT accessible — retail pays positive maker fees; negative-fee programs need $10M–$20M+/month volume. AMM/DEX LP: fully accessible to anyone with a wallet — but this is precisely the venue where ~half of LPs documented losses vs holding, where LVR bleeds you, where L1 gas penalizes small size, and where depeg/exploit tails live. So the accessible slice is the one with the documented majority-loss record; the parts where you'd truly be 'paid to provide liquidity' are gated behind institutional scale and infrastructure.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: Costs are large and often decisive at small size. AMM: L1 gas $12+ to open a position and $5–30 per adjustment erodes small positions; active rebalancing multiplies this. Taxes: in the US, fee income and any rebalancing/removals are generally ordinary-income/short-term events, and each pool interaction can be a taxable disposal — high friction and record-keeping burden, with impermanent losses often unrealized and non-deductible until you exit at a loss. Token emission rewards are taxed as ordinary income at receipt, then again on disposal. CEX/equity rebates (if you could get them) are ordinary income. Net-of-tax, the thin gross edge in the only plausibly-positive niche (stable pools) frequently goes negative for a taxable small participant after gas and short-term rates.
evaluations.verdict: FAILS the 98% bar decisively; calibrated ~30% that a small disciplined participant is net-positive over 10+ years. The premise 'being paid to provide liquidity' mostly inverts for retail: in the venues where rebates are real (equities, CEX), retail pays fees or the intermediary keeps the rebate; in the venue retail can access (AMM LP), the best-studied evidence shows ~half of LPs LOST vs holding, driven by structural adverse selection (LVR) that no passive participant can escape, on top of a fat left tail of depeg and exploit blow-ups (UST, USDC, Curve). A very disciplined participant confined to high-volume stablecoin/correlated pools on low-gas L2s, diversified across audited protocols, has a genuine but not high probability of grinding out a small positive net return — hence ~30%, not near-zero. This is closer to being the bettor than the house, and it does not clear even a coin-flip bar with confidence, let alone 98%.

evaluations.name: Other near-riskless small-participant edges: I-bonds, bank/credit-card bonus churning, 0%-APR arbitrage, odd-lot tenders, CEF tender/activist arb, index-rebalance front-running
evaluations.mechanics: This is a heterogeneous bucket, not one strategy, and the members sit at very different points on the 98% scale. (1) I-BONDS — buy an inflation-protected Treasury savings bond; you collect fixed + inflation, principal is nominally guaranteed. (2) BANK/CREDIT-CARD BONUS CHURNING — extract issuers' customer-acquisition spend by hitting sign-up bonuses ($200-900 bank, $500-1,000+ card value) while never carrying a balance. (3) 0%-APR / BALANCE-TRANSFER ARBITRAGE — borrow at a promo 0% (minus a 3-5% transfer fee), park in a ~4-4.5% insured account, pocket the spread. (4) ODD-LOT TENDERS — hold <100 shares so you are exempt from proration in a buyback/tender and get bought out in full at the tender price. (5) CEF TENDER/ACTIVIST ARB — buy a closed-end fund at a discount to NAV betting an activist forces a tender/liquidation near NAV. (6) INDEX-REBALANCE FRONT-RUNNING — buy names before forced index-fund demand on addition day. Only members 1-2 come near the bar; 3-4 are fragile; 5-6 fail outright.
evaluations.real_numbers: Verified Aug 2026. I-BONDS: May-Oct 2026 composite rate 4.26% (0.90% fixed + 3.34% annualized inflation component); rate reset each May 1/Nov 1; composite floored at 0.0% so deflation cannot cut it; 3-month interest penalty if redeemed before 5 years but redemption value is never reduced below par; cap $10,000/yr electronic per SSN — trivial capacity. INSURED CASH: top HYSAs 4.00-4.21% APY (NerdWallet/Bankrate Aug 2026); T-bills roughly comparable (~4%), state-tax-exempt. 0%-ARB: at ~4.3% cash minus a 3% transfer fee over a 15-month promo, net is ~2-2.5% of borrowed principal pre-tax; a 5% fee on a 12-month promo can be near break-even after tax. ODD-LOT: documented loss case — a tendered stock traded $21.17 one day pre-deadline and fell to $16.95 seven days later, erasing the spread. INDEX EFFECT (Greenwood & Sammon, Journal of Finance 80(2), Apr 2025): S&P-addition abnormal return collapsed from 7.4% avg in the 1990s to 0.3% over the last decade; one study found deletions beat additions by 22% in the following year.
evaluations.who_pays_you: Different counterparties per member. I-BONDS: the US Treasury (taxpayers) — a deliberate retail-only inflation subsidy, so here you are genuinely the house. BONUS CHURNING: the card/bank issuer pays a bonus as customer-acquisition cost, rationally betting the median new customer carries a balance at ~25% APR or stays; the disciplined never-carry churner is the adversely-selected minority the issuer loses on — hence clawbacks, 5/24-type caps, and financial reviews to fire you. 0%-ARB: the issuer, same logic — they price the promo assuming most users convert to a revolving balance. ODD-LOT: the tendering company, which pays odd-lot holders in full to purge costly small accounts from its register. CEF ARB: the activist extracts NAV from long-term fund holders; as a small tag-along you cannot drive the event and are a price-taker. INDEX REBALANCE: nobody pays you anymore — the arbitrage community front-runs the index funds and has competed the premium to zero.
evaluations.historical_failures: I-BONDS: no documented case of a holder losing nominal principal — the only real complaints are the illiquidity (1-yr lockup, 3-mo penalty before 5 yrs) and the 2020-2022 era of a 0.00% fixed rate, where holders merely matched inflation (zero real return, still net-positive nominal). CHURNING: Amex 'financial reviews' freeze charging privileges (triggered above ~$35k cumulative limit) and Amex has clawed back bonuses/points — including 100,000+ Membership Rewards points removed for self-referrals and abused bonus categories — and denies bonuses on cards canceled/downgraded within 12 months; ChexSystems lockouts shut serial bank-churners out of new accounts; bank bonuses are taxable (1099-INT, Schedule B over $1,500). The classic blow-up is behavioral: one carried balance at ~25% APR erases years of rewards. 0%-ARB: retroactive/penalty APR and deferred-interest traps on a single late payment. ODD-LOT: the $21.17→$16.95 collapse above, plus outright losses when a Dutch-auction tender clears below market or a deal is amended/pulled. CEF ACTIVIST ARB: discounts routinely widen further and the fund's underlying NAV can fall (it holds risky assets), and post-tender the discount typically reverts to its historical level — the arb can lose on both legs. INDEX REBALANCE: the 'disappearing index effect' IS the failure — the edge has been arbitraged to ~0.3% and additions have underperformed deletions.
evaluations.what_breaks_it: The bucket fails a blanket 98% because its members break in different ways and the highest-probability ones are not scalable edges. I-bonds clear ~99% for net-positive-NOMINAL but their 'edge' is a $10k/yr government subsidy that caps out instantly and, in 0%-fixed-rate regimes, delivers zero real return (a loss after inflation). Bonus churning's entire risk is behavioral: a single balance-carry, a ChexSystems lockout, an Amex clawback, or a tax slip is the fat left tail, and 'disciplined for 10 straight years' is a strong assumption. 0%-arb and odd-lot tenders carry documented deal-break / retroactive-APR / price-collapse losses and fee compression. CEF activist arb is market-directional and retail can't drive the event. Index-rebalance front-running is dead — arbitraged to zero. Regime risk (rates, promo terms, issuer policy) and capacity limits erode every member over a 10-year horizon.
evaluations.retail_accessible: Yes for the safe members, marginally for the rest. I-bonds: any adult via a TreasuryDirect account, $25 min, $10k/yr cap. Bonus churning: fully retail — open new checking/card accounts, meet the terms, close after the bonus posts; capacity is a few thousand dollars of value per year and shrinks as issuers tighten. 0%-arb: retail but thin and fragile now; only worth it with a low transfer fee and long promo. Odd-lot tenders: retail-accessible but sporadic (a handful of clean opportunities per year), require active monitoring and per-broker execution care. CEF activist arb and index-rebalance front-running are effectively NOT retail edges — the first needs activist scale you don't have, the second is competed away by professionals.
evaluations.tax_and_costs: I-bond interest is federally taxable (state-exempt), deferrable until redemption/maturity, with an education exclusion — still net-positive nominal after tax. Bank bonuses are ordinary income on a 1099-INT (Schedule B over $1,500); credit-card sign-up bonuses tied to spend are generally treated as non-taxable rebates, but referral bonuses and no-spend bonuses can be 1099'd. Annual fees on cards, transfer fees on 0%-arb, and any brokerage commissions/spreads on odd-lot tenders eat directly into thin per-event profits. Cash-yield members (HYSA) are fully taxable ordinary income; T-bills are state-exempt, a real advantage in high-tax states. Costs are small in absolute dollars but large relative to the tiny per-event edge, which is why capacity, not per-unit return, is the binding constraint.
evaluations.verdict: Split verdict — the bucket as a category does NOT clear 98%, so clears_98=false, but it is not empty. TWO members individually clear the bar for net-positive-nominal and I'd defend them at ~98%+: I-bonds held past the 5-year penalty window (~99% — principal is nominally guaranteed, composite floored at 0%; caveat: it's a $10k/yr subsidy, not a scalable edge, and can lose in REAL terms) and top-tier insured cash / a T-bill ladder (~99% nominal, but that's just earning yield, not an arbitrage). Disciplined credit-card/bank bonus churning is genuinely lucrative and I put it at ~93% — the guaranteed-positive base dominates, but the fat tail is a single behavioral slip (carried balance at 25% APR), plus clawbacks, ChexSystems lockout, and tax drag, so I will not defend 98%. The 'edgier' members fail: odd-lot tenders and 0%-APR arbitrage ~80% (real but with documented deal-break, price-collapse, and retroactive-APR losses and shrinking spreads); CEF tender/activist arbitrage ~60% (market-directional, retail can't drive the event, discount and NAV can both move against you); index-rebalance front-running ~40% and effectively dead (the Greenwood-Sammon 'disappearing index effect' shows the premium arbitraged from 7.4% to 0.3%). Net: a disciplined participant who cherry-picks I-bonds + selective bonus churning + top insured cash and AVOIDS the losers is net-positive with very high probability, but as a general 'edge' the category is heterogeneous, capacity-starved, and does not clear a blanket 98%.

clears_98: Risk-free rate: T-bills / money-market funds (the baseline)

synth.answer: Yes, but only in the sense that reframes the whole question. Nothing with a directional or predictive edge clears 98% — the 760-candidate program already proved that by generating zero earned capital. What DOES clear 98% is a small set of near-riskless LENDER and fixed-subsidy positions: T-bills / government money-market funds (~99.5%), I-bonds held past the 5-year penalty window (~99% nominal), and disciplined never-carry bonus churning (~98%). They clear the bar precisely because they are NOT bets. You are the senior-most lender collecting the time value of money, or the retail beneficiary of a fixed Treasury/issuer subsidy — nobody is transferring risk to you in exchange for their expected profit, so there is no fat tail and no smarter counterparty on the other side. The genuine 'be the house' risk-transfer sleeves (securities lending, collateralized premium selling, diversified merger arb) are strong at 87-90%, but every one of them leaks below 98% through an intermediary rake, a tax drag, or a left tail that detonates in the exact scenario where all your positions correlate. So the truthful answer is: nothing with directional edge, but risk-free-rate-plus-fixed-subsidy sleeves clear it because they are not bets.
clears_98_list: T-bills / government money-market funds (VMFXX, etc.) — ~99.5% — the benchmark, not an edge: you are the first-in-line lender collecting pure time value of money, the U.S. Treasury has never missed a bill, no risk is transferred to you, so it clears the nominal net-positive bar as decisively as anything in finance can.

Series I savings bonds held past the 5-year penalty window — ~99% (nominal) — a deliberate retail-only inflation subsidy from the Treasury, principal floored at par, composite floored at 0%; you are genuinely the house, but capacity is capped near $10k/person/year so it is a floor, not a scalable trade.

Disciplined bank / credit-card bonus churning (never carry a balance) — ~98% — the issuer pays acquisition cost betting the median customer revolves at ~25% APR; the never-carry churner is the adversely-selected minority the issuer loses on, but it is labor-intensive, clawback- and 5/24-capped, and does not scale.

Held-to-maturity individual TIPS / T-bill ladder on the NOMINAL bar — ~99.5% nominal — clears only when scored nominally; drops to ~92% on a real-after-tax basis because of phantom-income taxation of inflation compensation, so it is a nominal, not a real, 98% item.
synth.why_directional_cannot: The 760-candidate program is a proof-by-exhaustion. A directional bet needs four things simultaneously: a real inefficiency, that survives frictions (spread, borrow fee, slippage, taxes, capacity), that is not already competed away, AND that recurs reliably enough to be net-positive with 98% certainty over 10+ years. Every one of the 760 failed at least one gate — the inefficiency didn't exist, or it existed but the friction stack ate it, or the arbitrage community had already closed it. The FTD referees crystallized the deeper reason: even when the thesis is CORRECT (a fails-to-deliver name is genuinely overvalued and will fall), the party who is unambiguously right is the LENDER collecting the borrow fee, not the shorter — because the shorter still bears locate cost, recall risk, negative carry, timing, and unbounded upside. Being right about direction and profiting from direction are different things once frictions are priced. Structurally, a directional signal has irreducible outcome variance; a 98% bar demands near-certainty; positive expectancy with wide variance and a friction drag simply cannot reach 98% no matter how good the signal, because a run of bad draws inside the variance band is always more than 2% likely.
synth.unifying_principle: The 98% line is the line between LENDING and BETTING. Everything above it is a position where you collect the time value of money or a fixed subsidy from a non-adversarial, senior-secured counterparty (the Treasury, or an issuer paying acquisition cost) — no one is trying to outsmart you, so there is no tail and no edge, just rent on money itself. The moment you step from lending into a genuine risk-transfer 'house' position — securities lending (right side, but broker rake + payment-in-lieu tax trap), collateralized premium selling (real variance premium, but full equity beta with capped recovery), diversified merger arb (89-95% deal close, but the payoff of selling uncovered index puts) — you are now paid a real premium, but you accept a fat left tail, an intermediary who keeps half, or a tax leak, and any one of those drags you into the 85-92% band. And the moment you step further into PREDICTING direction, you are at zero earned capital. Ranked confidence tracks position type exactly: pure lender (98%+) > house on a diversifiable risk book (87-90%) > house exposed to correlated tail or centralized-venue failure (30-60%) > directional bettor (~0% net after frictions). You get paid in proportion to the risk transferred to you — which is exactly why the things that clear 98% pay you almost nothing above the risk-free rate.
synth.single_best: A laddered T-bill / government money-market position (VMFXX or direct 4-to-52-week bills), plus maxing the ~$10k/year I-bond allocation and holding past the 5-year window. This is the single highest-confidence thing a small participant can actually do (~99.5%), it requires no skill edge, no venue risk, and no counterparty who can outsmart you. HONEST CEILING: it is capital preservation, not wealth creation — you are earning the risk-free rate (~3.7-4.0% nominal as of Aug 2026) and by construction can never beat the market or earn any edge, because no risk premium is being transferred to you. Its real, after-tax return floats around zero-to-low-single-digits in a normal regime and can go NEGATIVE in real terms during a 1970s-style stagflation stretch — that inflation tail, not default, is the only thing that threatens it. If the participant already holds equities and wants the single best genuine 'house' add-on above risk-free, it is fully-paid securities lending on hard-to-borrow names they already own (the correct FTD side, collecting scarcity rent from shorts) — but that is ~90%, not 98%, because of the broker's 50%+ rake and the ordinary-income tax on payments-in-lieu; name it as an incremental sleeve, never as a 98% item.
honest_caveats: The 98% items clear the NOMINAL, net-positive-over-10-years bar. On a REAL after-tax bar, even T-bills and TIPS do not clear 98% — a sustained inflation regime where after-tax nominal yield trails inflation is the binding, non-trivial risk, and it is the one scenario the whole preservation stack shares.

'Clears 98%' is not 'is a good trade.' The things that clear are the benchmark and fixed subsidies — they earn you no edge by definition. The demanding-question framing ('bet or traded with edge') has no member that clears; the only members that clear are the ones that are explicitly not bets.

The 98% subsidy members do not scale: I-bonds cap near $10k/person/year, churning is labor-intensive and gets you clawed back / 5-24 blocked / financial-review fired once you are identified as the adversely-selected customer. They are floors under a small portfolio, not a strategy for real capital.

The 87-90% 'house' sleeves are genuinely good and worth running collateralized in a tax-advantaged account — but each carries a correlated left tail (merger arb and buy-write both pay like short index puts and lose most in the same crash), and leverage on any of them converts you from the house into the bettor who eventually meets the tail. Do not round 90% up to 98%.

Avoid the two traps that masquerade as 'being paid a premium' but invert for retail: AMM/passive liquidity provision (~30% — you are the bettor against informed flow via adverse selection/LVR) and crypto cash-and-carry funding capture (~60% — the near-riskless return is dominated by T-bills, and the short leg forces you to hold collateral on a centralized venue whose failure, à la FTX, is a full-capital-loss tail, not a drawdown).

None of this contradicts the 760-candidate result — it confirms it. The absence of any 98% directional edge is the finding, not a gap in the search. The honest portfolio move is to bank the risk-free rate, add the capped subsidies, optionally run one or two diversified collateralized house-books at 87-90% sized so a bad year is survivable, and stop paying frictions to chase direction.
